subsubtopic: ACCIDENTS TO LONGSHOREMEN-INQUIRY AS TO LABOUR CONDITIONS AND INSPECTION OF APPARATUS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) directed a question to me with respect to fatalities which had occurred in the harbour of Montreal and requested that I investigate and reply. On inquiry I find that since the opening of navigation three longshoremen have been killed in the loading and unloading of ships in the harbour of Montreal. Two other men lost their lives by drowning one a sailor and the other a longshoreman who was proceeding along the docks after his work had been finished. It would appear that neither of these two men was engaged in the work of loading or unloading ships at the time he met his death. I may add that the Department of Marine employs a tackle inspector at the port of Montreal whose duty it is to safeguard as far as possible those employed in loading and unloading ships by inspecting the apparatus used

for that purpose and by seeing that safe methods are employed.
It would not appear that the death of the three men killed while actually employed in loading or unloading a ship was due in any sense to defective apparatus. I would remind the house that fatal accidents are investigated by the coroner, and, in respect of each of the five cases mentioned, the verdict was accidental death. It is regrettable that in such a dangerous occupation as that of loading and unloading ships it seems to be impossible to avoid the occurrence of such accidents.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	The hon. member for Winnipeg
North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) addressed a question to me yesterday in connection with conditions affecting longshoremen in Montreal. I assume the information he was asking for has been given by my colleague, the Minister of Marine (Mr. Howe).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 88. Considerable inconvenience arose out of the original wording of the gift tax provision. The tax was payable at the time the gift was made, but the rate of tax on the individual gift was determined by the total of the gifts during the year, so that the situation arose that a gift might be made early in the year and the tax paid upon it, and by virtue of subsequent gifts during the same year the rate of tax payable on the first gift would be increased. That was the difficulty. A yearly payment of the tax is provided for by the amendment, and that will eliminate uncertainty with regard to the rate of tax payable, since at the end of the year the exact annual amount will be known.

4.	That gifts to any one person which in the aggregate do not exceed one thousand dollars in the calendar year be exempt from the provisions of the gift tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This bears on the point raised by my right hon. friend from Argenteuil. In the past exemption from the gift tax has been granted on a yearly aggregate of gifts up to $4,000, and it has been urged that this exemption is not sufficiently high because it acts as a deterrent to charitable giving. The purpose of the gift tax is to deter transfers of property, chiefly between members of a family, made with the object of reducing the amount of income tax which would otherwise be payable, that is, by putting it in a lower rather than a higher income bracket. It is not the purpose of the tax to deter charitable giving; that was not the original intention. This change is designed to encourage persons who for charitable reasons make annual gifts to relatives, dependents, former employees and so on, and is in the same spirit as section 5 (j) of the Income War Tax Act, which allows a deduction up to ten per cent of the total income for gifts made to charitable institutions. The $4,000 exemption will be retained but will apply only to the aggregate of gifts which individually do not exceed $1,000. That is to say, gifts of $1,000 or less shall not be regarded as gifts for tax purposes. Let me amplify that. Under the Income War Tax Act as it stands one may claim exemption up to ten per cent of one's income in respect of charitable contributions made to recognized charitable organizations. Under the gift tax provision as it has stood up to the present, if a man in a similar spirit of charity was supporting former

employees and relatives other than those in the exempted class he would nevertheless be taxed under the gift tax. It is thought that the spirit that prompted the house in 1930 to give recognition to gifts made to charitable organizations ought to be extended to cover the provisions of the gift tax in relation to gifts to individuals when the amount of such gifts does not exceed $1,000 in any one year.
A person may have dependents other than those mentioned in the act, as many of us have, and they may not be children or grandchildren. Few men reach an advanced age-

speechtext: Under the amendment the $4,000 exemption will be apart altogether from the exemption relating to gifts to any one person of $1,000. The object of the gift tax in the first place was very well stated by the right hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) when he said it was designed to prevent evasion of the income tax law by those who sought to make large gifts to relatives in order to bring their income tax into a lower bracket. That object is maintained. It has been in operation, I think, only one year, but in practice hardships have been demonstrated in connection with people who, while charitably minded, having a keen sense of their responsibilities towards former employees and distant relatives, are taxed on these charitable contributions. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Yes; I have an amendment in addition. The tax applies to films. It is found, however, that all films used in Canada are not copyrighted, and the purpose of this amendment is to ensure that payments for the use of all films, whether copyrighted or not, shall be subject to the tax. But since the original resolution was tabled the film producing companies have made representations and have demonstrated that a five per cent tax on gross remittances, which is what this particular tax is, is quite inequitable, in that it takes no account of their expense of production, and also would be unduly high. As few of the producing companies are making more than five per cent gross, we would be taking all of the income by the tax. The most important item of cost is the amortization of the cost of the negative and positive prints. The cost allocated to the Canadian business is on the basis of the number of positive prints used in Canadian distribution by comparison with the total number of positive prints used in world distribution. Therefore I propose by way of amendment to provide for a rate of allowance of sixty per cent from gross remittances, which is taken to represent the amortization of the film cost. In effect therefore the tax becomes a two per cent tax on gross remittances instead of five per cent as provided by the terms of the resolution as tabled. I am quite impressed with the representations made, and it was demonstrated to the satisfaction of the officers of the department that the proposal as originally stated would have had the effect of taking the whole gross revenue of these corporations-in some cases, not in all-because of the peculiar nature of their business. At the same time we do think we should have some

revenue from this source; hence this proposal, which I shall ask my colleague to move, providing that an allowance of sixty per cent of such payments may be made for the amortization of film costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The minister is referring solely and exclusively to personal holding companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Personal holding companies, in that connection. With regard to what may be called the general international concerns which incorporate here for any one of a number of reasons, whose assets are all over the world, we are giving them an option. They will be paying 7\ per cent and we think it is not an unfair rate to charge under the circumstances.

Does the minister think he will hold them here if he increases the rate from 5 to 7i per cent? I know of a number of such companies. Originally they were incorporated in Canada because of the security obtained under Canadian law. One large company of which I know was incorporated under the Canadian Companies Act after a conference of lawyers representing several international interests had examined the French law, the German law, and the United States law relating to the incorporation of companies. They preferred to seek Canadian incorporation because they felt that under the Canadian Companies Act there was greater security than there would be under certain foreign acts. Canada, therefore, was decided upon as the domicile of the proposed corporation. In so far as they declare and pay dividends to Canadians, if there are any Canadian shareholders, such dividends are entered by the recipients in their income tax returns, and therefore Canada obtains payment of the full amount of the tax. But in so far as such dividends are paid .to holders of stock in the so-called international corporation who are resident abroad, they are compelled to-day to pay not only the five per cent, which is withheld from them at the source in Canada, but also the heavy income taxes which are assessed by the several countries in which they may be domiciled. That is, a shareholder of such a company living, say, in a South American state would pay first the five per cent which was withheld at the source in Canada, and then the income tax in Argentina, or Brazil, or in France, or Great Britain. That makes the compensation which is paid by these shareholders for such security as they may obtain under the Canadian Companies Act or other act of incorporation in Canada, very heavy indeed in many cases. I suggest it is all to the good that the government should encourage the organization of such companies in Canada, and it seems to me that five per cent is a pretty heavy tax. If I

Income War Tax Act
were practising again in the profession-as I hope to do as soon as parliament prorogues, because I must earn a living-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Hear, hear. I must try to retain the hon. gentleman.
Mr. CAHAN -I think I would advise such clients who had in view the organization of a Canadian company to reconsider their position. I can find for them other states under the British crown in which they could incorporate and avoid these taxes; they could avoid the payment of the five per cent and possibly other heavy income taxes as well. The minister is running near the margin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With that I agree.

You are endangering the position, the citadel, it seems to me. I have great confidence in the astuteness of those who are administering the income tax in Canada. I have had something to do with them; they are very anxious to conserve the interests of the state and to ensure that the income tax is levied and paid. But we are getting very near the margin, and I think there will be fewer of these international companies incorporated in Canada hereafter under a 7j per cent tax than there have been in times past.

The minister's statement meets the situation to which I have had reference to a degree, but not wholly. I understand that something of this sort is done: A dummy company is formed; securities are transferred to that company; the owner of the securities receives non-interest bearing debentures. Therefore he receives no income from the property which is transferred. The income from the property is outside Canada. It is reinvested in non-interest bearing debentures and is treated as capital appreciation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is this a Canadian
corporation?

Yes. When funds are required, a formal sale of debentures is put through, by the people who organized the companies originally, and the result is that all forms of taxation are escaped. That is the information I have, and I shall be glad subsequently to supply the minister with details.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be very glad indeed to get such details, but I point out that in one particular at least the situation cannot be quite as my hon. friend understands it, because certainly a company formed as he suggests would itself pay income tax on its income. The individuals owning that company could of course leave the company's income in the company and thus
avoid personal income tax on receipts from the company, but offhand I cannot see how the company could escape taxation upon its own income. However, I shall be very glad indeed to get any information of that kind.

It is the duty and the privilege of this parliament to enact.laws to conserve dominion income derivable under the income tax, but I do not think there is any responsibility upon members of this parliament to concern themselves regarding the collection of income tax in Great Britain or the United States or any other foreign country. Those countries are very astute in the enactment of income tax laws under which they can obtain to the last cent full payment of the taxes which they levy. It is our duty to concern ourselves with the income of Canadians and to obtain such proportion of their income as is required for the purposes of the treasury. I have no hesitation, looking at it either from the political or from the moral point of view, in leaving foreign countries and foreign legislatures to enact such legislation as they may deem advisable for the purpose of preserving or increasing their revenues through their own income tax laws. If my hon. friend who has just spoken and raised the question has studied the income tax law of Great Britain, for instance, he must have found that the British parliament is very astute in making provision for the collection to the utmost possible extent of revenue derivable from the income of people domiciled in the united kingdom. That is not a concern of ours.
As to the moral aspect, in the practice of my profession I often adhere to the moral precept of an eminent English judge who says that there is no immorality in escaping an income tax that is not legally imposed by the law of the country. If it is under British legislation the income tax has to be interpreted strictly, but if it does not apply then there is no obliquity in endeavouring to escape from a tax that is not properly and legally applied. So I think we should be astute in looking after the payment of income tax by Canadians domiciled in this country, and not so astute in looking after the payment of income tax to foreign countries by those resident in foreign countries.
The hon. gentleman stated that many people in this country escape paying income tax. I do not accept his statement. If he has to do with advising clients as to the application of the income tax law he will find that in no country-none at least with which I am acquainted-is the income tax more strictly applied and more carefully collected than it is in Canada at the present time, and few escape.

Income War Tax Act

It was not with that
purpose in mind that I spoke, Mr. Chairman. My purpose was this: If we have large sums of British money in Canada that can be taxed but are not being taxed by Great Britain, then by all means let us tax them. If, on the other hand, Canadians who are making -large sums in Canada are using the laws of another country to escape payment of income tax, as perhaps some of these British people are in transferring their funds elsewhere, then I think it cuts both ways. We should look after these sums of money that are sent out of Canada to escape the payment of income tax. I am glad that the Minister of Finance has brought down this amendment.

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, what has been said by the previous speaker and others prompts me to say a word or two somewhat in reverse to what has been said this afternoon. For the last hour or two we have been discussing companies located in this country but owned by people who live abroad. I have in mind the fact that during comparatively recent years there- has been a tendency for wealthy Canadian financiers to make their domiciles outside of the Dominion of Canada in order to escape taxation, particularly income taxation. I do not know whether the action suggested by the minister as having been taken in Great Britain can be taken in this regard, but I think something should be done to prevent people who have amassed fortunes in Canada from making their domiciles abroad in order to escape what I would call their fair share of taxation. I should like to know whether the minister has given consideration to this aspect of the matter and whether he thinks anything can be done. I realize the difficulties that lie in the path of any minister of finance who attempts to do anything along these lines, but I do believe that when a person has amassed a fortune here and then leaves the shores of this country for the purpose of creating a domicile in some other part of the empire or the world, there should be some regulations under which the minister would be able to obtain from such a person the share of taxation which I think he ought to pay.

We might do as they do in Germany. As soon as a German, particularly one who is an Israelite, seeks to leave the country with his property, he is clapped in gaol and his international movements are then rather restricted. Unless some such law were introduced in Canada I am afraid it would be found very difficult to prevent Canadians from leaving this country and procuring a domicile in another country.

I am not suggesting that we should prevent anyone from leaving the country. He cannot take his property away with him; if he owns stocks, bonds or shares, it is most difficult for him to get rid of his holdings. All I am suggesting is that where a man has commercial interests in this country and makes his domicile abroad, when he has free access to Canada he should at least pay his fair share of taxation. I am afraid that the analogy given by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) is a very poor one.

I cannot accept the undertaking of the hon. gentleman, because I think it would be worthless. I think I know the situation as well as he does. For instance, the other day I had an application from a young man who had graduated in arts, I believe, and who had also graduated in engineering at McGill. He was anxious that I should assist him in securing a vocation. I asked him what income he wished. He thought that as he had spent so many years
at McGill he could not engage himself at a lower income than $3,000 or $3,500 a year. I told him of another young man in whom I had interested myself, who had also graduated in arts at a university, and in engineering, I think at McGill, and who wished then to obtain an income. My advice to him was that, if he desired to prosecute the profession which he had in view, he should engage himself with a certain hydro-electric company in the construction which was then proceeding of a station and a transmission line. I told him he would receive probably no more than enough to pay for his overalls and his board until he learned from practical experience to apply the education he had been acquiring over a period of seven years at the university. He accepted my advice and went to that company for a year. He then was quite willing to go on. He found out that the practical experience which he was acquiring would probably be very useful to him, and he came to me again. I secured for him employment for a year, during which he got his board and his overalls, with the General Electric Company in their testing department at Schenectady, and he spent another year there at that meagre income. Then he found that in order to qualify himself to compete for positions which would be open to him he required something more, and I got him employment with a large company in Pittsburgh engaged in the production of steel and iron structures. So he went for another year to learn from practical experience something about the testing of iron and steel for constructional purposes; at the end of the three years he was qualified for a position, and his services were sought.
Some of the young men who are graduating from our colleges are willing to qualify themselves in some such way, but many of them have been brought up since the war without any feeling of responsibility or appreciation of the necessity of qualifying themselves by training and experience for positions such as those of which I have been speaking. Under this item I should like to refer to a matter with the details of which the minister is familiar, and I should like to know what interpretation is placed on the statutes by those who have the last word. In July, 1919, it may be recalled, the Militia Pension Act was amended reducing from twenty years to ten years the period within which a member of the permanent force could qualify for pension, but this 1919 amendment was not made retroactive. Consequently those who had served less than twenty years prior to July, 1919, could not participate in the benefits of that amendment. In 1928 the Militia Pension Act was again amended, making retroactive the 1919 amendment, in so far only as it applied to members of the permanent force who were wounded while on active service and who were discharged as unfit for further duty. Now, I want to take you back more than one and a half years. In September, 1934, some three or four cases were reviewed under the 1928 amendment. I wish to refer to one of these cases particularly, because it relates to a man in my constituency. First of all, the application naturally went to the minister, and by him it was referred to the branch of his department which had to deal with it. That branch reviewed the man's period of service and determined whether he came within the terms of the amendment. Then the application went to another branch for the purpose of ascertaining his overseas record, whether he was disabled and discharged as physically unfit. I cannot speak for others but his application I know was approved by those in charge of the Department of National Defence whose duty it was to review these claims as to term of service and activity overseas. It was then handed to the minister and approved by him. From the minister it went to council and thence to the treasury board. That was in September, 1934. By the treasury board it was returned to the Department of National Defence for further explanation. It is still somewhere, nobody knows where; but when the government changed it was found among the items of unfinished business, and the minister then referred it to the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice ruled that they could find nothing in the statute to serve as a basis for refusing the pension. Now, is the man entitled to his claim or not? It seems to have taken one and a half years to determine it. It is a
statutory claim; the amendments of 1919 and 1928 are as plainly stated as it is possible to state them in the English or French language, and no definite reason seems to have been given anybody for not paying this claim. Furthermore this claimant received notice from the department that his case had been reviewed and submitted to the minister and that if approved he would receive his pension. What we would like to know is, by whom is it to be approved? Is the last word with the treasury board? The statute states clearly the terms and conditions under which the man is entitled to receive pension. You can well understand the anxiety of such claimants. The Department of Pensions disclaim responsibility, yet I think they have some responsibility, because the grounds upon which the man is entitled to receive pension are the fact of service overseas and his having been wounded; to that extent at any rate it has reference to the Department of Pensions. Here is a case in which the claim was approved by the minister's own officials, handed by the previous minister to the cabinet and passed on by the governor in council to the treasury board; then reviewed by the Department of Justice, which as I say found nothing in the act to serve as a basis for refusing the pension. The applicant seems io have fulfilled all the requirements of the Militia Pension Act, and I hope the minister will be able to tell us to-day who finally decides whether or not the man is to receive his pension.

Before the minister replies may I say in support of my hon. friend's contention that I remember this matter. In the short time in which I was Minister of National Defence it came before me twice. Would the minister mind if I took five minutes of the time1 of the committee to bring before it some facts that do not seem to be well understood by the house or the committee? It is about the superannuation of some people who have been seconded from the Department of National Defence to other departments. According to a return to an order of the house, there are three men in that position, General McNaughton, who is now president of the research council, Colonel Vanier, who is in England in the office of the High Commissioner, and Colonel Steel, of notorious fame, in the radio commission. The reason why the case of these gentlemen is brought to the attention of the house and the committee is not because they have been transferred, but because they have been seconded or loaned by the Department of National Defence to other departments. In the Militia Act there is a provision by virtue of which members of the staff of the Department of National Defence may be seconded instead of being transferred to other departments. What is the reason for that? The "why" is most important in this discussion. In fact, in one return the "why" was asked but was not given, and another return in which the "why" was asked has not yet been tabled. Each one of these gentlemen because he has been seconded from the Department of National Defence, to some other department, is entitled to superannuation which is twice as much as that to which he would have been entitled if he had been simply transferred. I want to bring very clearly before the mind of every member of the committee and of the minister, who knows the matter perhaps better than anybody else, that the fact that these three gentlemen have been seconded or loaned from the Department of National Defence instead of being transferred entitles them to double pension.
Last year in June, before the matter was ripe, the question was brought up in this house by you, Mr. Chairman, and also by the member for Temiscouata. We asked for some information from the government about it, and as usual the late government was entirely dumb; no answer came out of the mouth of the former Prime Minister or his colleagues. To me it seems shameful that General McNaughton and Colonel Steel, who are both members of the so-called head and brain trust of the late government, should be entitled to a reward which is twice as much as the pension to which they would have been entitled had they been simply transferred instead of seconded from the Department of National Defence to any other department.
I am strongly against that practice, and there is time yet for the Department of National Defence to bring these men back to that department and to superannuate them on the basis that would have applied if they had not been seconded. Is it not shameful to think that within six years General McNaughton will be entitled to twice as much pension as he would receive if he were retired now and were not brought back to the Department of National Defence? According to returns which have been tabled in the house General McNaughton has no office in the Department of National Defence, Colonel Steel has no office in the Department of National Defence, Colonel Vanier has no office in the Department of National Defence, but in spite of that, these people will take advantage of the fact that they passed through that department to receive twice as much for their superannuation in these days when salaries are cut by five per cent. I cannot conceive it, Mr. Chairman. Mind you, I have no grudge against General McNaughton, Colonel Steel or Colonel Vanier. I am discussing this question as a matter of principle, and I am doing it now because I believe that some members do not understand the situation. But it is very plain. It is explained in very easy language, the meaning of which can escape no one.

I wonder whether the
minister could give us some particulars about airports or emergency landing fields in British Columbia. There were several under construction last year, directly under this department, one at Hope and one at Boothroyd. I would also like the minister to deal with the Chilliwack airport.

I am quite familiar with the one at Chilliwack. There were certain difficulties in regard to that, with which I think my hon. friend is thoroughly familiar. A site was chosen by the former government I think, although I am not exactly sure about that, and certain difficulties arose with reference to the dyking charges. The whole situation was referred to the Department of Justice, which gave as a legal opinion that the virtual contract which

Supply-Defence-Civil Aviation
had been entered into previously was not binding because the dyking charges in question had not been revealed by the owners of the property. No final determination has as yet been made in regard to that specific piece of property. The whole situation is quite open at the present moment, and the department is considering whether to accept the virtual contract that was entered into previously or whether to look for a new property in the vicinity of Chilliwack. I may say to my hon. friend that I shall be only too glad to receive from him any recommendations with reference to that site.

I think the minister will recollect that I have discussed the matter with him. Since the difficulty developed I had an interview with these people when I was at home at Easter and they advised me that they had informed the official, who came there at the time and took the particulars, that there was a dyking charge. Apparently the owners considered that the person who bought it would continue to pay the charges just as the person who buys a piece of agricultural property continues to pay the taxes on it. It developed later, after the option was drawn up, that the dyking charge was in the form of a capital charge of $50 an acre. The purchase price plus dyking charges is very reasonable for 160 acres. The property is at the present time used as a landing field. It requires very little to complete it, and $150 an acre is very reasonable if you compare that with the cost of some other landing fields.
I was just going to ask my hon. friend: Does he consider that with the added charges it is a reasonable price to pay for an airport?

I think anybody would say that it is a reasonable price in comparison with that of others which have been purchased. The field is almost as level as the floor of this chamber. There are five or six planes using it now. The unfortunate thing about the matter is that this land is owned by a farmer, and had it not been for this purchase being in contemplation he would have broken the land this year and put in a crop, but he has held it. We are in hopes that something will be done.
There is another point about this matter which the minister, coming from the coast, will quite understand. At the time of the fogs on the coast the fog drops down within ten or twelve miles west of this airport, which was selected by the civil aviation authorities when they went through selecting landing fields on a direct route to Vancouver. The fog at certain times is so thick that it is 12739-2031
impossible to drive or fly through it. The airmen strike the fog within ten or twelve miles west of this site which has been selected; when it is impossible to fly through they have to return to the landing field, and if this landing field were not there they would have to go back to Hope airport, about thirty miles further east; the landing fields are supposed to be thirty miles apart. I would strongly recommend the government to take over this airport which would cost very little to develop, and is being used by five or six airplanes to-day.

My hon. friend throws a new light on the situation. He states that the official of the department who was there was made familiar with these dyking charges. This is the first time that has been brought to my notice. In the option that was given at the time these dyking charges were not included. The whole question now is this: With these charges, is this a reasonable price for the airport? My hon. friend says that it is the best site available. The whole situation is absolutely open and the department will be glad to receive any recommendations. As I have already explained, the situation was, I was advised, that certain incidental liens or charges had not been disclosed by the owners, and when the matter was referred to the Justice department they declared that the contract was not valid.
I understand that. I have a copy of the letter. The option expired in January.
Yes, so I understand.

I just wish to repeat that this site was chosen, I believe, by the officials of the air force branch of the department at the coast. They went over the line and considered this landing field to be on the direct route, and a natural landing field requiring very little work, and situated favourably east of the line where the fog breaks. When a farmer sells land to another farmer or anybody else and quotes a price of $100 an acre, he naturally expects that the purchaser will continue to pay the taxes on it, and the owners of this property told the official that there was a dyking tax and a municipal tax. They never considered it a capital charge, and I would have thought that the official would go into a little more detail with the provincial government. I know the minister is deeply interested in this landing field. It was chosen, not by the previous government-and I had no say in the matter-but by the officials of the department who picked out these landing fields.

The minister went from
Grand Forks to Kitchener, and I take it for granted that Salmo field will be completed. There has already been expended upon this field something like $63,000, a larger amount than has been expended on almost any other field. I should like to ask the minister if the policy of this government is to be different from the policy of the former administration with reference to assistance to municipal air ports. There has been $63,000 expended on the Salmo airport and apparently it is not completed. The policy of the previous government with reference to assistance to municipal airports was to permit men to go from the relief camps to do this work. In the case of the Trail airport, this would have involved transportation of twelve miles both morning and evening as well as the erection of dining halls and other buildings. This would have cost the town far more than the assistance would have been worth.
I have referred already to the fact that Trail is entitled to more than ordinary recognition. This is practically the only field between Winnipeg and the coast where planes
can obtain repairs. More than $25,000 worth of repairs was made at this field last year. It is the only field between Winnipeg and the coast where radio service is available to the arctic circle or any other part of Canada for twenty-four hours in the day. This field is on the direct line of the airway as well as being on both the Great Northern and the Canadian Pacific railway lines. Actually there is more export mail leaving Trail than there is leaving any industrial point in the dominion. I hope the government can see its way clear to changing its policy in order to provide a more direct method of betterment for these municipal airports.

I agree absolutely with my hon. friend's reference to the progressiveness of Trail, not only in connection with the facilities provided for flying but in connection with the officials of the Consolidated Mining & Smelting company who have done so much in the way of pioneer work. One of their officials recently received the McKee trans-Canada trophy for the greatest success in flying in the dominion. With regard to assistance for municipal airports, my information is that direct contributions have never been made. My information also is that the former government offered assistance to the Trail airport as an unemployment relief project, but that offer was not favourably considered. Again I say that I agree with my hon. friend that there are no more progressive facilities provided in Canada than those at Trail.
The proposal was to bring men from a relief camp some twelve or fourteen miles from Trail, and the town would have had to provide living quarters.

There is a direction finding station ten miles north of Brandon at Forrest. It has not been operated recently. There is a civic airport at Brandon, located at the northern boundary of the city, and it has gone into receivership. The minister will have received a letter dated May 15, a copy of which I have, asking whether the government would consider taking over that airport. There are 187 acres as level as the floor of this chamber, with a hangar and a few other buildings, and that airport is well worth considering, for it is in the direct line of flight as you go west from Winnipeg. I should like to see it given some consideration.

My hon. friend is in the same position as the hon. member for Kootenay West. Brandon is just as progressive as Trail, but unfortunately is not on the direct route as laid out by the

technical officers of the department. That route was laid out some time ago and was not under my auspices. However I can promise that every possible consideration will be given my hon. friend's representations.
Do I understand that it is the intention of the department to change that direction finding station north of Brandon? It is in the direct line of flight, this airport being seven miles to the south.
That was not the intention, but I shall be glad to give the matter every possible consideration. A deviation of seven or eight miles in direction finding is material.
Is it intended to finish the Trail landing field this year?
I am informed that it is an intermediate landing field, and as far as I am aware it is not the policy to consider it in any other light.

Can the

Reverting to the discussion that took place before recess with regard to the purchase of aircraft equipment, I find in a return tabled by the minister that tenders were called for in connection with the following: two Fairchild machines; two Waco "S6" aircraft; one Stinson "SR-7B" aircraft. One Moth was purchased from de Havilland Aircraft Limited, Toronto; six fleet aircraft, from Fleet Aircraft of Canada Limited; eight Avro Avian planes from the Ottawa Car Manufacturing Company; two Fleet Trainor aircraft from Fleet Aircraft of Canada Limited and two Fairchild aircraft from Fairchild Aircraft of Canada. Why were not tenders called for in all instances for the purchase of new equipment, not including the purchase of secondhand equipment?

As regards airplanes, tenders are necessarily governed by the type of plane required, and the element of competition is not present in all cases. There might be one type of plane required for strictly military purposes, another type of plane for training purposes, which would be entirely different, and possibly a third type of plane for ordinary civil aviation

or transportation purposes. I was under the impression that tenders were called for in every case but I am advised that that is not so, but the prices of all types of aircraft are known in the department.

The fact that $4,130,000 has been voted for the Royal Canadian Air Force, an increase of 81,000,000 over last year's vote, and only $1,262,000 odd for civil aviation, an increase of only $511,406 over last year's vote, prompts me to make a few observations regarding what I consider a serious inconsistency. I find that during the years of depression this parliament has voted various sums exceeding in total $122,000,000, and it is interesting to contrast that with the contributions from the federal treasury for relief purposes, about which there has been so much criticism, amounting to $160,000,000. In my opinion all we have now as a result of that enormous expenditure by the department is what the officers of the force themselves describe as a bow and arrow army and a teakettle navy. As regards the aviation branch, something which is in the initial stage of development in Canada, I suggest that as far as possible we should avoid the mistakes which have been made in the past and see to it that this branch is not cluttered up with the obsolete traditions from which the military and naval branches have suffered in the past. We are asked again this year to vote, apart from the item now under consideration, some $25,000,000-and in that amount I include the votes for the various buildings and the votes made available for national defence through the supplementary estimates-all representing a substantial increase over the vote of last year. It seems to me that this should be subjected to the most rigid scrutiny. The minister has said that this appropriation is for purposes of defence, but I may say in this house-and my opinion is corroborated by many men with expert training in military matters-that this is simply a $25,000,000 cardboard front as far as defence purposes are concerned, a cardboard front behind which there operates to a large extent a social patronage racket.
When we come to aviation we find that civil aviation is sacrificed to the military branch, which is not competent to any degree to assume responsibility for the technical training of young men, and so far there has been no indication from the minister that the department is prepared to undertake technical training of the nature required. Surely any military expert will agree that under present conditions there is nothing more urgent than technical training, from the standpoint of defence, if the nation desires defence.

Supply-Defence-Civil Aviation
In the various aviation clubs across Canada we have a very efficient organization. The young men associated in these clubs, the minister will agree, are making a notable contribution to the development of aviation in Canada. Much of the important research work which is necessary is being conducted under the auspices of this organization, and as far as I can discover it is the one agency by means of which young men may find some opportunity to secure technical training and to keep abreast of developments in aviation in the world to-day. They are eagerly and enthusiastically taking advantage of that opportunity as far as they are permitted. From my personal experience the majority of the instructors attached to the flying clubs are rendering the country admirable service and doing whatever is possible, under the serious handicaps from which they suffer, to promote aviation in the way in which it should be promoted having regard to the development of our country.
In connection with the purchase of equipment I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the general staff of the department who decide this matter are apparently palming off on our flying clubs equipment that is so obsolete that if they accept it at the present time, under the regulations, as I understand, for at least three years they cannot possibly secure access to modern equipment or obtain instruction in blind flying and in the latest aids to aerial navigation which are now being brought out. This is a policy radically different from that which has been sponsored by the British air ministry. Let me refer again to this particular purchase of equipment indicated in the return I mentioned previously. These planes are described in an article in the current issue of Cavalcade. The eight planes are Avro Avians with Genet-Major engines:
A type of light aeroplane that has not been built in Canada since 1929. Their motors are five cylinder 100-110 horsepower. Their speed is only 100 m.p.h. Their carrying capacity is 458 pounds.
Three years ago the last Mark IV Avians were washed out as obsolete by the Royal Canadian Air Force. This year the government of Canada has bought eight of the machines for issue to civilian flying clubs and paid $3,498 apiece for them. The Ottawa Car Manufacturing Company was the vendor. No tenders were asked. The Hon. T. P. Ahearn, who contributed substantially to t'he victory of Liberalism, is president of the Ottawa Car Manufacturing Company. I am not at the moment particularly interested in that angle, but I have before me an advertisement which appeared in the issue of
March, 1933, of Canadian Aviation, and in which these same Avro Avians, I understand, were advertised at "a new low price record." The advertisement reads:
The Avro Avian can now be purchased on the deferred payment plan and offers a saving to prospective aircraft owners never before equalled. Fifteen hundred dollars cash payment and you can own a new Avro Avian with Armstrong-Siddeley Genet-Major engine, 100110 h.p. The balance you "pay as you fly" in twelve monthly instalments of $140 each.
The advertisement goes on to say that these planes are "completely modified."
In every respect the purchaser of an Avian is the owner of one of the most up to date, Canadian-built, light aeroplanes suitable for training, sport and commercial use. Write for further particulars. Sole Canadian manufacturing and selling rights, Ottawa Car Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Ottawa, Canada.
The government paid the sum of $3,498. That, I submit, is not giving civil aviation the encouragement it deserves, particularly in view of the splendid record established in this branch by young men attached to flying clubs in this country. I feel that the government made a decidedly bad bargain. These machines were listed at a lower price in 1933 and intervening years. Surely they have not appreciated in value since that time. It is unquestionable that they are hopelessly outdated for purposes of aviation instruction at the present time; that they are obsolete from every point of view for such uses. Furthermore, the safety factor enters in, for if these machines have been in the stock of the Ottawa Car Manufacturing Company for seven, eight or nine years, having been purchased in the boom years when it was anticipated that there would be a remarkable development of aviation, it stands to reason that the wooden struts and the fabric in these machines must have deteriorated, and not even the most rigid inspection under the auspices of government inspectors can guarantee that they are airworthy for purposes of instruction. After all, machines used for these purposes stand considerable rough usage.
The point I particularly wish to stress is that these machines are obsolete, and in providing them for flying clubs-and there is no indication in the return tabled 'by the minister that anything but obsolete machines will be furnished to the flying clubs-the department is seriously handicapping this work. It is of little advantage to this country to vote large sums of money for the development of flying fields if the young men who are interested in the technical development of the industry are in this manner precluded from keeping abreast of modern technical requirements.

I cannot pit his judgment or my own against that of the inspectors of the department, who are qualified to pass upon such matters.
My hon. friend also said that civil aviation was being sacrificed to military aviation, and spoke about some other hon. gentleman's reference to a bow and arrow army and a teakettle navy. May I suggest that it does not help our situation in Canada for anyone to cast aspersions upon the nation's attempt to get something effective for the defence of this dominion. Some persons outside this house have made similar comments in various publications. I believe their intentions were honourable and sincere; that they were trying to mend matters, but to cast aspersions upon the adequacy of our forces is like trying to plunge a dagger in the back of this nation. As long as I am in charge of this department I am going to do the very best I can to fight for the dignity of the department and for its 
personnel in all three services, and I am going to strive as best I can, with my colleagues in this government, to see that the defence department of Canada gets a decent show in the next four years; that our navy gets a chance; that our air force get a chance, and that the personnel of our militia and our permanent force are also properly supported. I regret very much that my hon. friend thinks fit to cast continual aspersions upon the adequacy of the military aviation of this country. In our military aviation branch we have excellent men. In Canada we have men unsurpassed in the entire world. During the great war, as my hon. friend knows, Canada led the whole world on the battlefield; her soldiers blazed the name of Canada in immortal letters across the forefront of the world; and to-day some of them are still giving of their time, their knowledge and their enterprise to build up a creditable aviation service in this country. So I say that, no matter what our private opinions may be, we should strive to the best of our ability to support this work. There is nothing militaristic about it. We are trying to build up, not to tear down, aviation and in the naval and military branches, not for attacking purposes but purely for purposes of decent and honourable defence if an unfortunate necessity should ever arise. I must deny my hon. friend's suggestion that we are sacrificing civil aviation. For the first time in six or seven years we have increased very materially the vote for civil aviation. We are convinced that our policy is a progressive one, leading to the development of civil aviation and not sacrificing it for the sake of military aviation. I am surprised that my hon. friend, for whom I have a profound regard, should be continually making these attacks upon the defence forces of Canada, because I can tell him that every member of this government is as profoundly and sincerely attached to the processes of social reform and the advancement of the masses as he is. But at the same time this government is charged with the responsibility of looking after the defences of this nation, and so long as I am in charge of this department I am going to fight for the advancement and the maintenance of adequate defence forces in this dominion.

In the defence which has 'been -made by the minister, one point has not been explained. I have in my hand a copy of Canadian Aviation for March, 1933, and, as was stated by the hon. member for

Supply-Defence-Civil Aviation
Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), these same planes were advertised on the basis of a cash payment of $1,500 and $140 a month for twelve months, making a total price of $3,180. Now we find, three years later, that the planes, with three years' deterioration, are bought by the government of Canada at three or four hundred dollars more. That is one point which has not been explained. It has been stated that had an offer been made last year they could have been obtained for less than the price advertised in 1933.
I listened to the minister's impassioned defence of the department, and I listened also with a good deal of interest to what my colleague in this comer of the house said. On no occasion did he attack the men under the department. He was attacking certain things in connection with the department that should be brought to the attention of the government and the members of this house. As one who is interested in civil aviation and who has done a good deal of flying, I want to say that in my opinion if Canada is to develop flying men-and flying women for that matter-the equipment used should be modern, up to date, and in the best possible condition.
The point I wish to make is this, that an explanation has not been given as to why the dominion government paid this amount for planes three years after they were advertised for sale at lower prices. And may I say that in the advertisement which I hold in my hand it is definitely stated that these machines will be thoroughly modified to suit any requirements. The question is why the government of Canada bought planes built in 1928 and paid considerably more than the price for which they could have been bought three years ago by private individuals, singly and on a time payment basis. That is the point.

The
answer is very simple: They were not the same planes. When completed, the planes were specially reconditioned, and therefore the price was different.

I admire the eloquence with which the minister has defended the department, and I appreciate just as sincerely as he does the necessity of dealing with this problem in a rational, sane way, always having in mind possible eventualities. But I pointed to the fact that during the years of the depression we spent in excess of $122,000,000 for national defence, and we had a right to demand efficient methods of defence. If the people of this country desire that the government should prepare for war, for heaven's sake let us prepare for war and let us expend this money in the most efficient manner possible.
I have no apology to offer to the minister for begrudging every nickel that is taken from the starving unemployed and devoted to the purpose of national defence, but I know that in Canada we do not enjoy a scheme of national defence which is commensurate with the millions that are being spent, or shall I say squandered, for that purpose in this country. While the understanding of the minister may be as he has expressed it in this chamber, I cannot help thinking that his opinion is based upon what he has been told by the general staff, from whom he must take advice. I believe there are many ex-service men in Canada who will join with me in expressing some lack of confidence in some members of that staff, in that they have a desire to build up an elaborate organization, and no doubt have some very plausible reasons for the necessity of such an establishment.
I realize that I am introducing a grave question, but I do so in sincerity. I will ask the minister to consider the possibility of Canada having to play her part in a world war to-morrow, in conflict with some of the great powers of the world. One of the first requirements would be to find young men physically well developed. The late Sir Arthur Currie made that point time and time again, and I am not casting aspersions on the personnel of the Department of National Defence when I say that the department, following out-dated traditions, is entirely disregarding its responsibilities in this connection. One has only to inspect the various parades of the militia units and see the hollow-chested youths who are in the ranks of these parades to realize that they are not given the physical training necessary to make them fit for the emergency which I hope we may avoid. Another and still more urgent consideration, under the mechanized conditions of modem warfare, is that the young men should have technical training. Bayonet practice, which is very largely the instruction they are getting in these elaborate barracks we are building here and there across the country and in the training camps, is not giving them the technical training necessary in order that we may have men who understand how to take down and reassemble all the elaborate mechanical equipment that will be employed in the war which apparently is looming before us. I am not casting aspersions on the personnel of the department when I say that in clinging to these old traditions they are not assuming any responsibility in this vital regard, and I ask the minister where, at the moment of emergency, for purposes of defence, will he find young men with the necessary technical training.

Supply-Defence-Civil Aviation
I have no reverence for the halo of gold braid and red tabs that seems to hang around a military establishment, making it impossible for a layman to offer any sensible criticism. I have not forgotten the bitter experiences through which many of us went in 1914 and 1915 by reason of the ghastly and tragic mistakes made by the general staff, men who had occupied these comfortable offices for years and had not kept abreast of developments in military tactics. It is commonly stated that it was the man in the ranks, Tommy Atkins himself, who in a very practical way forced upon the attention of the general staff the fact that more practical methods were possible. If Heinie was in a hole over there and Tommy Atkins was in a hole over here he knew he could not reach Heinie with a bayonet, but if he filled a tin can with a little gun-cotton and a few rusty nails he could and did bomb Heinie out of that hole. So you can trace the development of these tactics to which the general staff was blind.
I am taking the minister on his own ground, that of national defence, and I am pointing out that the policy of the department as it has been conducted is not affording this country any reasonable assurance that for the money expended it is receiving adequate value in national defence. On my own responsibility I express the opinion that the present military establishment, because of the manner in which it is organized

with the non-permanent active militia split into some 443 units, for example-is not satisfactory. I say this criticism that has been offered by the president of the Canadian Infantry Association, for one, and by other men whose articles have recently appeared in Canadian periodicals, is justified because the mechanism is antiquated and could not possibly be equal to the emergency if we should be called upon to defend ourselves.
So I do not think the minister has any reason to take me to task for casting aspersions, nor do I think he has any right to suggest that I am stabbing Canada in the back when I criticize the existing system of national defence. I am quite as sincere and earnest about this matter as the minister is himself, and as a member of this house I think I have a perfect right to suggest that for this enormous expenditure, over $25,000,000 this year, the Canadian people have a right to demand full value by way of a defence organization.

I find
my hon. friend strangely inconsistent. He is now advocating what I announced a few days

ago as the policy of the Department of National Defence, the reorganization of the Canadian militia; that has been advocated by every defence association, infantry, artillery and the others in the Dominion of Canada. I want to explain to the committee, in regard to those who proffer advice to-day to this department, it does not matter whether it is under a Liberal or a Conservative government or even if it were Cooperative Commonwealth Federation government, that the technical officers of the department are as good as any men in the world. The specialists of the Department of National Defence are in touch with every process of military training in England and in every country in Europe. We know every process of mechanization, and the only reason we have not been able to carry out such processes in Canada is because we have not had the financial resources. The minister has made a spirited defence of his department. I think I can bear out all he has said with regard to the way in which the department is now run. In view of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) I feel it my duty to say a few words on this occasion. I happen to have been one of those who went overseas in the ranks of the Canadian forces and served as a sergeant for some time; I have some knowledge of the training of the first contingent on Salisbury plain and then on to the front. It has also been my privilege since the war to be in command of one of the regiments. While I respect very much the viewpoint of the hon. member for Vancouver North, and believe he is sincere in what he has said, yet I think it is hardly fair to call in question the splendid efforts that so many young men of Canada are making to-day in joining the militia. If the training they- are getting is not adequate to the day-and I think perhaps it is not-the minister has indicated the reason. I also think it strange that the hon. member for Vancouver North, in view of the attitude which is taken by those associated with him with reference to preparing for military defence, should question the present effort to bring our forces to such a measure of perfection as may be possible.
Remembering that the day may come when our Canadian youth may have to take part again in modern warfare, as they did in 1914, it is a serious matter to assume the responsibility of not making those men ready for that eventuality. It is easy to charge militarism, but I submit that there are few men who served in the front line overseas who are really possessed by any spirit of militarism in these matters. I unhesitatingly say that we owe an obligation to the youth of Canada to see that if the day ever comes that they again have to face the reality of actual warfare, they have officers and non-commissioned officers sufficiently trained that the men will not have to pay the penalty in physical suffering or with their lives for that lack of training. We owe it to youth to train them to understand the instruments of warfare which they may have to use. That cannot be learned in a day or a month. One of the essential things for fighting men is that degree of training

The situation is as follows: When I was entrusted with the responsibility of this department, I had some consultation with those who are responsible for the direction of policy. While I agree with my right hon. friend that this position was not filled for several years, I considered that it was my duty to place the gentleman at duty. He was eminently qualified to survey the industrial potentialities of Canada, and to make a complete national industrial survey, and I am glad to say that substantial progress has already been made. The duties are set forth in King's Regulations and Orders for the Canadian militia as amended by general order No. 12 of February 1, 1936. These are the duties as reclassified, following almost in toto, I am informed, the language of the appointment in Great Britain. In other words, the duties formerly carried out by the chief of the general staff and by the quartermaster general have been reassigned in this reclassification to the master general of the ordnance. My profound conviction is this, that there is nothing more necessary in the Dominion of Canada than the work which is being carried on in that office now. I found this-and I am certain that my predecessors found it also-that while the personnel of the militia, the air force, and the navy are splendid, the situation with reference to equipment is simply tragic. The duties of this officer are to survey the entire situation, the rifle situation, the situation with regard to all kinds of armament and all kinds of equipment, with reference to the necessity some day of the Dominion of Canada itself taking over the entire production of all equipment of arms in case there is national trouble, because I am a profound believer that private individuals and private firms should not be entrusted with the manufacture of armaments. I must say I am. I accept absolute and complete responsibility for this appointment. I make this statement to this committee: Not a single soul made a recommendation to me with reference to Brigadier Caldwell. I submit I have kept away from partisan considerations in considering the estimates of the Department of National Defence because I think this is the one department which should be kept absolutely free of partisan considerations. I regret very much that my right hon. friend, who made such a noble and inspiring speech in London last night, should attribute political motives to a man who is just trying to reorganize a service and do the best he can. I believe the retirement of Brigadier Caldwell was a mistake. It was done without his consent, but that was not the reason I took him back. I took him back because I realized the necessity of the reorganization of the industrial resources branch and I take complete and sole responsibility for the appointment. As a matter of fact, I am certain I have rendered a service to the Dominion of Canada and possibly future development will prove that I am right.

I suppose there has never been a more disconcerting example of an injurious effect upon the service. Let me put to the minister what he would have said if he had been on this side of the house. Here is a man who was retired. He is gazetted as being retired. The order in council was passed in 1934 and he was entitled to ten months' full pay and allowances without service, having earned this. There is a change of government and the whole morale of the department is at once shot by this man being put back into a position which had been abolished since the death of General Morrison. That is the situation. What is more likely to have a serious effect upon the morale of that department? The minister says that I should not make these statements because I have an interest in these matters, but that is why I am making them. I cannot conceive of anything more calculated to make it at once apparent that the department is no longer being conducted on the basis of merit, but that it is being conducted on the basis of political pull.
Brigadier Caldwell's politics were well known. I am glad to hear the minister say that no one had anything to do with the appointment except himself because that places the responsibility where by law it belongs. This man received nine months' pay without doing anything for it, and I ask the minister: What is being done to offset such an example in the department? I say that the course pursued is injurious to the morale

of the department. I merely say to the minister that the general view of those acquainted with the facts is that this is a bit of political jobbery. He assures us that nothing but the highest of motives and an earnest desire to serve the state synchronized with the possibilities of Brigadier Caldwell being available for the job, and that this synchronization brought about his reappointment to a position that had not been filled for nearly ten years; and it is now to be filled by one whose peculiar qualities are that he had been retired on nine months' retiring allowance and full pay.
I congratulate the minister upon his loyal exposition of the reasons that brought about the result, but I cannot give him a very strong recommendation for the judgment he has exercised. For I think he would have no difficulty in selecting at least half a dozen -and I think I could name them to him- who would be more sprightly and would be better qualified to discharge the duties to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I only mention that, because I have no desire to do more than get the explanation on record. It is useful for many purposes, among them as showing how spasmodic the love of economy is and that, like lightning, it does not seem to strike often in the same place. Before we carry the last item, which has been held over, there are just a few general remarks I should like to make with regard to the Department of National Defence. My colleague from Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) has been charging obsolete equipment and obsolete methods, and I would go a little bit further than that and venture to suggest that war itself is an obsolete method of trying to settle international disputes. And for that reason, when these National Defence estimates are under consideration, we might at least once a year ask the more fundamental question as to what we are getting as a result of this enormous expenditure.
The minister has said that the policy of the department is not necessarily a policy that changes with a change of administration. That, I suggest, is really the trouble. We have inherited a military establishment and a theory of national defence and we have not stopped to examine the efficiency of that establishment or the soundness of the theory. In an article I read a short time ago in the Ottawa Journal, taken from the Financial Post, the writer states that the cost of the war has amounted to a grand total of $4,341,488,904. Now, that is the cost in dollars and cents, which, as the Minister of Finance confesses, is a major factor in our budgetary difficulties to-day; and none of us can estimate the cost in human wastage and the disorganization of society that has taken place.
Feeling this way some of us can hardly sit quietly year after year without at least uttering a protest against the continuance of a policy which is not bringing results. I know that some members of the house simply hurl at us the epithet "pacifist," and they think that this settles the matter. Well, I suppose it is easy for us to retort that they are militarists. But I do not know that this sort of thing gets us very far. I know we all want peace; that is taken for granted. But I suggest that we differ materially on the question as to how to attain peace, and under these circumstances those of us who have a theory other than that which is generally held by, I believe, the majority in this house, regard it as our duty to try to state our position.
We have heard it said to-night that there should be no party divisions in a matter of this kind. I suggest that in the days to come this matter of national defence, inextricably intertwined with the question of foreign policy, must become a political issue; there is no way out. Indeed, it should become a political issue because the people to-day are no longer united as to the efficiency of this method or attempted method of arriving at national
[Mr I. Mackenzie.)
security. We talk sometimes about fire protection. I can quite understand that it is all very well for us to come and talk about fire engines and ladders and hose and things of that sort; but if we are living in a city of jerrybuilt frame houses; if we have no proper wiring arrangements, no building inspection, it is manifest that though we maintain an efficient fire brigade and have finely equipped fire engines and all the rest of it, that will not prevent our city from burning down. We have to approach the matter in a far more scientific way. And so I want to ask this minister, as I have asked previous ministers, exactly what the policy of his department is.
The minister said not long ago at a meeting of the Canadian Artillery Association:
In my mind there are two cardinal and guiding principles to be borne in mind when establishing a system of national defence. First, we must have defence forces sufficient to control subversive elements from within, and secondly, to repel attacks from without.
The other day in making his statement of policy-and I commend him for having done this-he made no reference whatever to this point which he regarded as of primary importance, namely, to take care of the subversive elements from within. I am not going into that matter to-night, but I point out once more that if we give our people a decent chance we shall not need very many policemen and we shall not need any military organization. I state that as my belief and the belief of a large number of people whom I am trying to represent.
We are to repel attacks from without, we are told. I am sometimes accused of being an idealist, but to-night I should like for a few minutes to be very practical indeed. I would ask the minister and the house whether we expect any European country to attack us. Would Germany attack us? Would Italy attack us? I do not think for a moment that the great United States to the south of us, with its Monroe doctrine, would permit anything of the kind. You may say: Well, but you are simply depending upon another nation. I am not particularly concerned with what the implications of all that kind of thing may be, but I submit that if we are thinking about some foe from Europe we are putting up a hypothesis which has no basis in fact. Do we expect Japan to attack us from the oriental side? I would say that there are many other countries nearer at hand upon which Japan might cast envious eyes. And again, the United States, with its Monroe doctrine, would not suffer any invasion of the north American continent.

But if they did want to attack us, does any sane man believe that we, with a small population of ten millions, could stand out against a population of 120 millions; that we, with this great army that we hear so much about, so splendidly equipped, would be able to hold out against the armies of the great republic to the south of us? The United States does not want to attack us; there is no doubt of that. Then against whom are we really arming? Are our defence forces to defend us against any possible enemy? Again I say, no. I think it was the minister who said the other day that we ought to have reasonable preparation for the defence of our country. Have we reasonable preparation to-day? I cannot think we have reasonable preparation whereby we can stand alone against any enemy that might attack us.
From another angle altogether than that which has been presented so far, I ask: Are we justified in spending these large amounts with the idea that they really give us security? The minister went on to say that we have certain League of Nations' commitments. I should like to know where we stand in that regard. I have asked the Prime Minister, and so far he has declined to tell the house what our commitments are, and whether or not there are any understandings.
Does the hon. member want to start a war?

I think it is a most extraordinary position for the government to take. Mr. J. M. Macdonnell recently had a letter in the London Times, in which he suggests that Canadians might be divided roughly into three groups with regard to foreign policy: those who believe in isolation or security through their position on the north American continent; those who still maintain pretty much the attitude that most people had in 1914, that is that we are an integral part of the empire and must rush to the empire's assistance; and those who place some reliance, at least, upon the League of Nations or cling to the idea of collective security. If we in Canada are so divided, is it not about time that the Canadian people knew at least where the government stands on this matter? I think it is. I think we ought to know from the government-

No.

About the British empire; that is another matter.

Since the passing of the statute of Westminster the dominion may make any laws it likes, regardless of whether they conflict with British laws or have effect outside the borders of Canada, provided only that they do not conflict with any limitations imposed by the British North America Act. The conduct of foreign relations, being a matter governed by royal prerogative and not by statute, was unaffected by the statute of Westminster. The governor general in Canada represents the king and exercises the royal prerogative by delegation for the purposes of the dominion government. His powers are set out in the letters patent and instructions which govern his office, to which have been added certain other powers by constitutional usage. The conduct of foreign relations, however, is not included in these powers. Every Canadian treaty above the level of a mere convention or trade treaty must be ratified personally by the king in London. To put the matter in a nutshell, Canada has now full control over her own legislation, but not full control over the executive functions of her government. What is needed is to round out her control over the executive function in the same way that the statute of Westminster rounded it out over the legislative function.
It has been suggested to me by some legal friends whom I have consulted that this might be done in one of two ways. In the first place new instructions might be issued to the governor general stating specifically that he had power to represent the king in every aspect of the domestic or external affairs of the dominion, such power to be exercised on the advice of his majesty's ministers in the dominion. In other words, Edward VIII might delegate the whole of the prerogative to the governor general instead of merely a portion, as at present. This simple act involves no legislation and no amendment of the British North America Act. At the same time it probably would be necessary to give the governor general a great seal to be affixed to all treaties and documents dealing with external affairs. Such a seal is now possessed by the governors general in both the Irish Free State and the Union of South Africa.
