In 1934 the Union of South Africa secured for herself precisely what Canada now lacks; in that year, by the Status of Union Act and the Royal Executive Functions and Seals Act, the union parliament declared that:
"The executive government of the union in regard to any aspect of its domestic or external affairs is vested in the king, acting on the advice of his ministers of state for the union, and may be administered by His Majesty in person or by the governor general as his representative;"
They provided the governor general with a great seal and a royal signet, and they added the following provision:

"6. (1) Whenever for any reason the king's signature to any instrument requiring the king's sign manual cannot be obtained or whenever the delay involved in obtaining the king's signature to any such instrument in the ordinary course would, in the opinion of the governor general in council, either frustrate the object thereof, or unduly retard the dispatch of public business, the governor general shall, subject to such instructions as may from time to time, in that behalf, be given by the king on the advice of his ministers of state for the union, execute and sign such instrument on behalf of His Majesty, and an instrument so executed and signed by the governor general and countersigned by one of the king's ministers of the union shall be of the same force and effect as an instrument signed by the king."
The proposed step would therefore place Canada on terms of complete constitutional equality, not only with Great Britain, but with her sister dominions of South Africa and the Irish Free State.
This proposal might perhaps better have been made on the more general question of external affairs. But I have ventured to deal with it to-night because I feel that the outstanding weak spot in our relationship with Great Britain is the fact that if Great Britain were involved in war we might automatically be regarded by other nations as being at war. Our shipping might be attacked. Conceivably the United States might undertake to invade Canada. That is highly improbable of course, but I speak of the constitutional aspect. In that case Canada would simply be a second Belgium. I remember a strong Conservative saying to me several years ago that if any such contingency arose the only thing for Canada to do would be immediately to declare her independence. This gentleman was not only a Conservative, but a very strong imperialist. However, I think he viewed things in a practical way. Now I do not think that situation is fair to Great Britain. If Great Britain became involved in a European war I do not think it would be fair for us at the very last moment to say: We are not going in; we will stay out. Although the hour is
late there are some statements made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. MacNeil) that should not be permitted to remain on Hansard without at least some attention being paid to them. I can quite understand that the minister, having been held up by Mr. Wayling as a model of St. George about to engage in mortal combat with the dragon, might hesitate to controvert the declarations of Mr. Wayling, but I am sure that no member of this committee has a clearer appreciation of the unsoundness of the statement that has just been read than the member who has just taken his seat. To compare war conditions with militia conditions in Canada is an insult on the part of Mr. Wayling to the intelligence of the Canadian people. Just think for a moment what the position is. Why did the militia come into being? If one goes back to the days of Sir George Cartier, he will find the story of it. The Militia Act in essence was to extend to every part of Canada the opportunity for those who so desired to train and constitute a part of the active militia of the country, and that is the reason that it is scattered over every part of Canada.
Mr. Wayling suggests that in the war the regiments were at strength. Of course they were. That is the job of recruiting, the job ultimately of conscription, to maintain the units at strength. The reason the militia units are not at strength is obvious, and it may not be unattributable to just such discussions as have taken place in the house during the lastr few days, and to attacks such as that made by Mr. Wayling.
I put it to any member of this committee: What would you think if you were asked to compare the regiments of the Canadian army in France and England with the skeleton units that are scattered all over Canada, and then were asked to say that because there is only
a skeleton unit of the militia forces in this country at the present time, therefore there is too much fat in it, the militia, and it should be cleaned out and cut down to the number at full strength that existed during the war. No one but Mr. Wayling would possibly have made an argument such as that. A columnist who is paid by the column always does that because it has to be padded up with a semblance of fact, a semblance of a semblance of fact. It is made to appeal to every possible kind of prejudice and passion in those who take a certain view with respect to a matter of this kind.
Our militia goes back to the days of Cartier.
I believe he piloted the first Militia Act through this house. One section of that act has never been changed since the time it was put upon the statute books; that is the section with respect to the necessity of consultation by parliament before there could be any possible chance of Canada engaging in hostilities outside the defence of our own country. Why is it that we have a unit in Nova Scotia, another in New Brunswick and others in the different military districts throughout the country? Why have we one in Quebec? Why is it that on Sundays we get over the radio the music of the band under Captain Gagnon? Why is it that we have these military districts across Canada? Why is the minister, according to the daily press, establishing a new one here in Ottawa? This is done in order that in every section of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific there should exist the nucleus of some militia unit. It might be engineers; it might be artillery; it might be a machine gun corps; it might be a medical corps, it might be infantry or cavalry; they are all nuclei of units being maintained in the different sections.
Anyone who is familiar with the story of the enlistments in this country knows that the back-bone of all our efforts in 1914 was the militia. My hon. friend is so well informed that I would hesitate to express an opinion which would contravene his, but certainly the relations that existed between the efforts made under Lord Haldane to organize the territorials in England, which were so very successful, and the efforts made in this country were not wholly dissimilar. Certainly General Gwatkin, then Colonel Gwatkin, did an unostentatious service to this country. He remained in his office under protest when he desired to join his unit and go to France and Flanders. His work was of the first character and I can only say that when Mr. Wayling endeavours to compare non-comparable things he does a disservice to this country.

I refer to this article because it is unfair to our fellow-Canadians who are offering themselves for the defence of their country.
I repeat that the whole policy of the territorials in Great Britain and our militia here is to maintain in every section of the country, even in the remotest, some skeleton organization that will permit of men enlisting for voluntary service. There is one question which the minister has not cleared up to-night and in connection with which I should like to make some brief observations. This is with respect to the relations between our country and the other 
units of the British empire. In 1926 agreements were arrived at for the purpose, not of massing troops, but to make available to the different countries of the British empire information as to the best means of training or as to the type of armament that might be available or the best forms of mechanized effort that could be used. Communication of the information that came to the staff in Great Britain through their efforts was made to the staff in Canada, to the staff in Australia, to the small staff in New Zealand and to the staff in South Africa, so that in every part of this far-flung empire there might be the fullest possible information as to the latest development in the means of defence, in mechanized armament and in the use of the human element in the maintenance of the defences of the country. I understand that this has been going on steadily.
I happen to know, and those who are familiar with the literature of the day will recall, that the efforts made by Lord Haldane to develop a staff, based as he frankly said upon the German example, led to his being able, when he went back to the war office- this will be found in his autobiography and I daresay many hon. gentlemen have heard him say it himself-at the instance of Mr. Asquith, to call the appropriate official and ask him if any change had been made since he had last been there. When he found that no change had been made he was able to dispatch telegrams which brought about within a few hours the mobilization of what was known as the first expeditionary force, sometimes referred to as the Old Contemptibles.
My understanding is that that policy is maintained in this country so far as staff work is concerned. All information as to the use of mechanized armament together with the use of the human element is available to Canada in the fullest possible sense. There has been an exchange of views between the general staffs as to whether or not these matters could not be more publicly discussed, but the view of the general staff in Great Britain, as communicated to the staffs of the various overseas dominions, was that these were naturally confidential, and were communicated only for their guidance and assistance in matters of this kind.
The minister is carrying on the difficult work of endeavouring to modernize to the fullest possible extent, with a limited income, the defence forces of Canada. The late government was not possessed of sufficient money to enable it to do what it would have liked to do in that regard, and we said that financial conditions made this impossible. I am glad

I was pointing out that by universal consent, the result of study from the earliest dawn of history until the present day, there must be a combination of two factors to secure the life of a nation. The purpose of this-I repeat it-is to ensure our being in a position if needs be to have at our hand such equipment as would enable us adequately to defend our country and its institutions; whether the attack against them comes from without or from within, the law contemplates that force being available for either end. That is what the law is, I said.

I also

believe that one of the reasons why Great Britain has been spared in these recent years the turmoil which has occurred in some other European countries is because the British people have always taken that particular attitude.

And naval.

And a naval demonstration. But may I add this: the good sense of the British people at that time overcame the dangers of that demonstration. I do not think that in any other country in the world that kind of thing could have happened. But in Britain, from time immemorial, people have believed that military forces were not to be used to suppress their fellow citizens who had legitimate grievances. If the excuse for military preparations is the preservation of our institutions, of course that is a different matter. But, as one who is fundamentally opposed to the use of force, particularly in connection with the making of necessary social and economic changes, I wish to point out to the committee that a great deal of colour is lent, by statements such as those to which I have referred, to the propaganda of those who believe, quite conscientiously, that force will ultimately be involved. One other thing. I desire to support my hon. friend from Vancouver North (Mr. Mac-Neil) in regard to the dissatisfaction which he says exists among a good many men connected with the militia, and to make this contrast. I have before me the figures expended in relief during six years of depression, amounting to about $162,000,000 prior to May a year ago, and I also have before me a statement of the amount spent on militia and defence from 1929 to 1936, amounting to $122,000,000. What do I find? That practically for every four dollars spent to relieve distress, some three dollars were spent in military preparedness. These are astounding figures. Though, as is sometimes said, Canada faces a grave situation on account of expenditures

Supply-Defence-Ordnance
on behalf of the unemployed and to relieve distress, we make military expenditures involving sums of money almost as large, even in these years of depression, as we make to relieve distress. I am in agreement with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that Canada's best defence at the present time is its defencelessness. I am not going to develop that thought, but in my opinion a country the size of Canada, with its diverse peoples and small population, is best defended if we rely upon our weakness physically and our goodwill as a good world neighbour, rather than attempt to ape the military powers of the European countries.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 61, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into Committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Application to companies incorporated after 4th May, 1910.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The only amendment is the inclusion of the words "except as hereinafter otherwise provided" in both subsections.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Retroactive subsection.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I have some little
doubt about this part of the bill. It is an exceptional exercise of power, as I pointed out the other day, to have parliament declare that a certain act has been in force since 1910. I can understand difficulties in connection with a particular session, that the date should relate back to the opening of the session or something like that, but I must say that I think this section goes-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Very far.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Yes, and further than I would care to go. If the minister has made up his mind that this is a proper exercise of power I am not going to say anything further about it, but these words seem to go very far:
Every special act of the parliament of Canada passed after the 4th day of May, 1910, for the incorporation of a company ... shall be read as if it contained the provisions hereinafter in this section set forth....
That is, in the creation of a company it is said that since that date these provisions have applied. That seems to me to be most unfair. To say that it applies from to-day is simple, but to say that a corporation created in 1911 should have attached to it and to its officers responsibilities which then were non-existent from the standpoint of legislation is going a very long distance. Perhaps the minister might state the necessity for this. The note of explanation is not quite clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: It is not really complete.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It is good as far as it
goes, but I should like to know just what pressing necessity brings about a request that parliament should exercise a power so extraordinary. It is going back twenty-six years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I must say that I had
the same view when I first read this section; I held my breath and wondered at our learned brethren in another place proposing such a thing, but the explanation helps to some extent, in that the retroactive amendment in respect of companies incorporated since 1910 makes effective the provisions intended to be incorporated by references in the special acts of incorporation. All such companies have been incorporated under a model form of bill varied, however, in many cases to suit special circumstances affecting the company. The section of the act providing for the model bill did not contemplate am

Canadian and British Insurance
variations therefrom, and in the opinion of the parliamentary counsel of the senate the variations introduced in some special acts may have the effect of depriving the companies of the benefit of certain provisions of the act essential for the organization of the companies. The essential portion of the amendment is the insertion in section 5 of the act of the words, referring to the model bill, or in that form varied as such special act shall provide." Far be it from me to quarrel with the opinion of the parliamentary counsel of the senate that this retroactive amendment, so far from being restrictive, really removes doubts as to the powers of companies.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes, but the other side of the question is the phase in which I was interested, the imposition of responsibilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes, but of course in that connection we must take into account the words "or in that form varied as such special act shall provide."

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: In view of what the minister has said I can only repeat that this is a most extraordinary power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: It is.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The argument the minister has presented to the committee is perfectly sound. That is, if a company was compelled to be incorporated in accordance with the model bill, and was incorporated not in accordance with the terms of the model bill, it might well be, having regard to the language used, that if that company attempted to exercise powers other than those contained in the model bill there would be some difficulty. But the answer is that parliament is omnipotent, and parliament has seen fit in special cases to clothe companies with powers other than those mentioned in the model bill. It must be taken that parliament is at least fairly sensible in the exercise of its duties, so these words must be read in accordance with what has been said, as a first canon of construction, so as to give common sense to the general terms that were used. I appeal to my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott), toho, according to report, is so soon to grace the judiciary; I am sure he will agree with me that parliament must be taken to express consistently a common sense view of the legislation. Here you have an act not strictly in accordance with the model act. Parliament passed that act, presumably with its eyes open.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Of course the words "or in that form varied as such special act shall provide" would come in there.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Those are the new added words, and that is said to be retroactive for twenty-six years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes. The opinion of the parliamentary counsel of the senate is that they make certain that the special act shall apply.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Quite so. I just put this case, and then I will not take up further time. If parliament saw fit to create by special act a company, and the powers conferred upon that company were less or more than those named in the model bill governing such companies, now to go back over a period of twenty-six years and say that the company shall be governed by the provisions of this act hereinafter mentioned is to do a most extraordinary thing. If the minister who is charged under the statute with responsibility for the administration of the insurance act thinks it is desirable, however, I am not going to labour the point at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I asked precisely the
questions my right hon. friend has indicated, particularly from the point of view of retroactive legislation. Of course I was especially careful to ask if any institution could be prejudicially affected and the answer given to me was that the insurance companies were represented before the banking and commerce committee of the senate by an eminent counsel, in the person of Hon. N. W. Rowell, I believe, and that this was not questioned there by any of the companies. In fact I was assured that some of them asked for it, although I do not know why.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Annual meeting to be at the head office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
This is just relating one
section to another.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Approval of bylaws by treasury board.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The approval of bylaws
by the treasury board has been in force since the passing of the last insurance act some few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. BENNETT.:	Although we did this
I always doubted the advisability of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The value lies, I think,
in a report from the superintendent of insurance, with respect to such bylaws, to the treasury board.

Canadian and British Insurance

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: The point was not that. Ultimately the report of the treasury board goes to the governor in council. Just what point there is in putting the superintendent of insurance in between, I could never quite understand, because it is not like the administration of the treasury in the old country, where the treasury board stands for something entirely different from the one here. I suppose this is merely to connect the two sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is all.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Lending funds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Section 5 is for the purpose of making sure that the limits imposed by section 60 of the act on the investment in common stocks may not be effectively doubled by loans on such stocks, in addition to the amounts permitted to be invested therein.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is at the instance of the superintendent of insurance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Power to invest in stock of other insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Section 6 simply contains the amendment contained in subsection 1 of the next preceding section.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I do not think we should pass this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Section 60 imposes two limitations on investment in common stocks. The first limitation is that common stocks to be eligible for investment must have paid dividends of at least four per cent per annum or $4 per share per annum for seven years next preceding the date of investment, and that the investment in the stocks of any corporation shall not exceed thirty per cent of the total stocks issued. The limitations in this subsection have been in force since 1910.
The second limitation is contained in subsection 6 of section 60, and limits the percentage of the assets of any company which may be invested in common stocks to fifteen per cent. This limitation was first proposed in 1932.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: We did it because of a specific case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
In the amendment of 1927 the limitation contained in subsection 1 of section 60 was overridden by an amendment to section 61 of the act to permit companies
other than life insurance companies to invest a certain portion of their funds in the common stocks of other insurance companies, even if those stocks did not comply, as to dividends or as to the percentage of the total stocks invested in, with subsection 1 of section 60.
. The limitation now contained in section 6 of subsection 60 had not then been enacted, and therefore section 61 overrode all of section 60.
With the introduction in 1932 of the limitation now contained in subsection 6 of section 60, section 61 should have been amended to make it clear that subsection 6 was not also overridden by the amendment of 1927 to section 61. This, however, was not done, and the amendment now made by section 6 of the bill is to make it clear that section 61 overrides only subsection 1 of section 60 and not subsection 6 of section 60 as well.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Putting it shortly, the . minister might have said that it simply provides that "notwithstanding anything herein contained an insurance company other than a life insurance company can buy shares in any other insurance company regardless of whether they have been paying dividends continuously or not."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Other than a life company.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes, this does not touch a life company. If it did I would have no doubt that my duty is to oppose it. Having regard to the constant complaints that are being made about the centralization of power in the hands of a few, which often are wholly unsound, this does lend itself to support that argument, because it enables a fire insurance company or any other form of insurance company other than a life insurance company to acquire shares in any other kind of insurance company, life insurance or otherwise, notwithstanding the fact that it may not have paid dividends during the prescribed time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: My right hon. friend appreciates that there is no intention of changing what has been the law.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: But as a matter of fact, as the law stands now, they cannot do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Is it not rather a matter of doubt?

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I would hardly put it in that way. I think parliament intended, judging from its temper at the time it passed the law, that they should not do it. I do not say that with any certainty. In 1932 I personally had to do with the matter; in 1934 the then Minister of Finance was dealing with it.
3206	COMMONS
Canadian and British Insurance

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I am quite willing to leave the bill in committee on that.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Is that the last clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: No; there are several more, but we have passed the controversial ones. I do not want to press something which should be given further consideration. Perhaps it would be well for me to confer further with the superintendent of insurance on that matter, although I am fairly clear what his object is.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: I put this to the minister: A large and powerful fire insurance company knows that a life insurance company has not been paying dividends during the last few years, and that it has really been in some difficulty having regard to the great decrease in values of common stocks, so it conceives the happy plan of acquiring control of that enterprise. Under this section it could do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is, a fire insurance company could.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: A fire insurance company could acquire control of a life insurance company. As the law stands to-day, it could not do so. When this bill passes it would be possible for it to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: That was not my impression, but I should like to consult the legal authorities.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Mark you, a life insurance company could not do it, but a fire insurance company could acquire the shares of a life insurance company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
We might rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again on this bill.
Progress reported.
